original_test_intent: Verify that a controlled BIOS system-date change persists across save/reset into setup and is reflected correctly in the OS, then restore the original authoritative time policy without harming time-dependent services or evidence.
original_method: Capture BIOS/RTC, BMC and OS clocks plus timezone/NTP ownership; choose an approved bounded alternate date; pause competing synchronization; change and save BIOS date; verify after reset and OS boot; then restore authoritative time and synchronization and validate chronological health.
manual_activity: Operator or validated console enters BIOS, changes only the date to the approved value, saves/resets, verifies setup readback and exits; owner approves temporary clock disturbance and restoration.
required_inputs: Approved temporary date and maximum skew
Impact review for logs, TLS, authentication, jobs, leases and databases
safety_requirements: Require approval before changing time and resetting
Preserve logs instead of clearing them
Check active jobs/users and time-sensitive services
Record all clock surfaces before change
Do not confuse BIOS Release Date with system date
Control competing synchronization under approved policy
Stop on unexpected clock jump, boot or authentication failure
Verify log chronology and service health
agent_execution_scope: Present exact old/new date and reset plan
Coordinate read-only console navigation except approved date change
engineer_actions: Approve temporary date/skew and maintenance window
Provide BIOS console steps and recovery

command_applicability.original_deepseek_command_fit: `dmidecode -t 0` Release Date reads BIOS image metadata and cannot exercise BIOS system-date entry, save/reset persistence or OS RTC reflection. sshpass and disabled host-key checking are unsafe.
command_applicability.command_recommendation: With exact values and approval, capture all clock surfaces, pause only the approved synchronization owner, change BIOS system date, save/reset, verify setup and OS/RTC readback with timestamps, then restore authoritative time and synchronization.
command_applicability.original_parameters_and_time_preserved: BIOS Main-page date, alternate-date change, save/reset, setup/OS checks and 5/5-minute timing are preserved; values, timezone and sync policy are not guessed.

modernized_recommendation.recommended_method: Use a clock-correlation ledger with monotonic timestamps and BIOS/RTC/BMC/OS wall clocks before change, after reset, after OS boot and after restoration.
modernized_recommendation.difference_from_original_method: Adds time ownership, service impact and complete restoration around the original UI workflow.
modernized_recommendation.coverage_difference: Distinguishes BIOS persistence from NTP auto-correction and detects RTC, timezone and cross-clock disagreement.
modernized_recommendation.risks_limitations: A wall-clock jump can invalidate TLS, leases, authentication, scheduled work and log ordering even when the BIOS field behaves correctly.

project_override_considerations: The referenced TPM script and DeepSeek BIOS Release Date command do not cover this testcase. Only the mutable BIOS/RTC system date and its OS reflection are in scope.
expected_evidence: No hardware PASS claim by the agent

source_conflict_analysis.analysis: Items, procedure and criteria consistently target mutable BIOS system date and OS reflection. The unrelated script/DeepSeek command is a review mismatch, not conflicting Master intent.

blocked_analysis.analysis: The date-change operation, impact controls and restoration are identifiable finite inputs. Execution is blocked only if time ownership or safe restoration cannot be established after request.

review_improvement: Prevents immutable firmware Release Date from passing a mutable RTC/date-persistence test and controls system-wide risks from clock changes.
independent_technical_reasoning: BIOS setup date normally writes the RTC, while the OS may reinterpret it under UTC/localtime policy and immediately correct it through NTP. Therefore persistence must be observed before automatic synchronization obscures the result, using monotonic timestamps for sequence. Because the operation changes time and resets the host, explicit confirmation and restoration make REQUIRES appropriate.
